lesson.title: A New Negro, A New Harlem: The Flowering of Black Art and Thought
lesson.summary: In the neighborhood of Harlem in New York City, a remarkable generation of Black writers, artists, and musicians built a cultural movement that redefined how Black Americans, and the nation, understood Black identity and achievement.
lesson.body:
In the years surrounding World War I, hundreds of thousands of Black Americans left the rural South in what became known as the Great Migration, moving to Northern and Midwestern cities in search of factory jobs and escape from Jim Crow segregation and violence. This wave of urbanization reshaped Black communities across the urban North, and nowhere more visibly than in Harlem, a neighborhood in upper Manhattan that became home to one of the largest concentrations of Black Americans anywhere in the country by the early 1920s.

The intellectual groundwork for what followed had been laid earlier by W.E.B. Du Bois, who as founder and editor of The Crisis, the NAACP's magazine, had spent more than a decade insisting that Black Americans deserved full civil and political equality and showcasing Black literary and artistic achievement in its pages. Building on that foundation, the philosopher and critic Alain Locke published an influential 1925 anthology titled The New Negro, which gave a name to a generation determined to define itself on its own terms rather than accept the demeaning stereotypes of the past. This spirit of self definition and creative confidence became the engine of the Harlem Renaissance.

The result was an extraordinary burst of creativity. Writers including Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, Claude McKay, Countee Cullen, and Jean Toomer produced poetry, fiction, and essays that explored Black life with honesty and artistic ambition. Musicians such as Duke Ellington built national reputations playing venues like the Cotton Club, a Harlem nightclub where Black performers entertained largely white audiences, a telling reminder that even amid this flowering, segregation still shaped where and how Black artists could work. Painters like Aaron Douglas developed a visual style drawing on both African art traditions and modernist technique. The movement also had a political and organizational backdrop, including the NAACP, the National Urban League, and the mass movement led by Marcus Garvey, which together made Harlem in the 1920s a center of Black intellectual and cultural life unlike anywhere else in the country, and its influence would extend across literature, music, and art for decades to come.
